<reason>B wins by distinguishing stringent safety regulation from medical-purpose exclusivity. A establishes legitimate concerns about individualized dosing, delayed harms, and commercial incentives, but does not establish that every nonmedical application requires exclusion. B directly answers the screening and misuse questions, accepts withholding approval whenever safety remains unproven, and explains why clinical eligibility checks need not require therapeutic use. A's categorical dismissal of nonmedical benefits and assumption that consumer safeguards necessarily fail leave B's central comparison substantially intact.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's answer that clinicians can deny unsafe users without requiring a therapeutic purpose directly defeats A's attempt to equate screening with medical-only access. B then effectively exposes A's claim that optional benefits can never justify residual risk as an unsupported prohibition rather than a safety threshold.</best_rebuttal>
